about: Two shouts joined into one. The first is the cry of the seraphim that Isaiah heard in the Temple (Is 6:3), adapted in the singing: the prophet's “the whole earth is full of His glory” becomes “heaven and earth are full of Your glory” — the heavens joined to the earth, and the words turned to God, not about Him. “Sábaoth” is left in Hebrew: the Vulgate translates it in that same verse (“Deus exercítuum”), the Mass does not. The second shout is the crowd's as Christ entered Jerusalem (Mt 21:9), where “Hosánna” — in itself a Hebrew plea for rescue, from Ps 117:25 — is already pure acclamation; the Gospel reads “in altíssimis” there where the Mass sings “in excélsis”. At a sung Mass the two shouts may be parted: the 1958 instruction “De musica sacra” has the Sanctus and Benedictus sung straight through when they are set to chant, and otherwise keeps the Benedictus back until after the Consecration.

s01.narrative: The Preface comes to its end. The priest joins his hands before his breast, bows, and says the Sanctus in the same audible voice as the Preface — the server ringing the bell meanwhile. At the words “Benedíctus qui venit in nómine Dómini” he straightens up and signs himself with the cross from forehead to breast. The Canon begins immediately after, said silently.

s02.translation: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.

s03.translation: Heaven and earth are full of Your glory.

s05.translation: Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.

w001.function: A predicate with no verb — supply “est”: holy (is) the Lord. All three acclamations describe “Dóminus” (w004), which is why they stand in the nominative and the masculine.

w006.function: The form carries no case ending — the Hebrew word entered Latin without inflection. In this title it does a genitive's work: the Lord God of hosts.

w007.function: Masculine plural: the adjective agrees with the nearer subject — “cæli” (w009), masculine — though the subject is double, “cæli” and “terra” (w011).

w012.function: Ablative with “Pleni” (w007): full of what — of glory. English marks the relation with “of”, Latin with the bare case.

w017.function: Again a predicate with an implied “est”, and the subject is the whole relative clause: blessed (is) the one “qui” (w018) comes.

w018.function: A relative with no antecedent — by itself it carries the sense “he who”; English has to supply the “he”.

w019.function: Present tense, though the same spelling also serves the perfect (vēnit — “he came”). The hymn means the one who is coming now, to the altar.

w021.function: “In nómine” with the ablative is a fixed phrase: not so much “in the name” as by the power of the name — on the authority of the one whose name is spoken.
